performers: Sviatoslav Richter, Warsaw National Philharmonic Orchestra, Stanisław Wisłocki
intro: Sviatoslav Richter plays the first movement, Moderato, of Rachmaninoff’s Piano Concerto No. 2, Op. 18. The piano opens with a series of chords, then plays arpeggios beneath the orchestra’s first melody.

sections.label: Intro · Piano chords over low F
sections.mNote: Repeated piano chords crescendo from pp over a recurring bass note

sections.label: A · Strings in C minor
sections.mNote: The piano’s arpeggios accompany strings and clarinet.

sections.label: B · Piano melody in E♭
sections.mNote: The piano plays a long melody after its running accompaniment

sections.label: Dev · Themes pass between piano and winds
sections.mNote: Short phrases pass through changing keys

sections.label: A′ · The tune returns against a march
sections.mNote: The orchestra sings while the piano presses forward in chords

sections.label: B′ · Solo horn in A♭
sections.mNote: The second theme returns over quiet string chords.

sections.label: Coda · Meno mosso, then C minor
sections.mNote: The first theme returns softly before the final acceleration.

relations.label: The first-subject music returns
relations.basis: The first subject and its associated material return in the recapitulation with changed piano writing. The excerpts lie in the later part of the opening subject group and its returning continuation, rather than at the large climax itself. CENS diagonal mean 0.931, sustained 14 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 369.5 s (cache/form/rachmaninoff-concerto-2-moderato.txt, candidate 2; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: Solo piano introduction
cues.text: The orchestra is silent. The piano plays a chord, drops to a low F and starts again. The chords grow louder from pp towards f, and the first theme enters after them.
cues.evidence: Gutheil full score, Boosey & Hawkes reprint, p. 3: solo piano introduction, recurring low F and poco a poco crescendo. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/72/IMSLP528309-PMLP01953-Rachmaninoff_-_Piano_Concerto_No._2_(orch._score).pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First subject in C minor
cues.text: Violins, violas and clarinet play the C minor melody. Beneath them the piano plays broken chords up and down the keyboard, and cellos and double basses play the bass notes pizzicato.
cues.evidence: Full score, pp. 3–4, rehearsal 1: C minor first subject, piano arpeggios and pizzicato lower strings.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Dr Nikolai Dahl, 1900
cues.text: “You will begin to write your concerto.” In the first months of 1900 Dr Nikolai Dahl repeated that promise to Rachmaninoff during their daily treatment sessions. After the failure of his First Symphony the composer had been struggling to write. The new concerto carried Dahl’s name on its dedication page.
cues.evidence: Marc Mandel’s BSO note quotes Dahl’s words to Rachmaninoff, dates the daily sessions January–April 1900 and documents the dedication. https://www.bso.org/works/piano-concerto-no-2-6

cues.title: Second subject in E♭ major, piano
cues.text: The piano plays the long second melody in E♭ major. The melody lies in its upper notes, over its own broken chords, and the orchestra plays little around them. The piano accompanied the first theme; here it plays both melody and accompaniment.
cues.evidence: Full score, first movement’s second subject and continuation, pp. 12–15; the E♭ major piano theme is also described in the work’s structural overview. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._2_(Rachmaninoff)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Development section
cues.text: The long melodies are broken into shorter phrases, which the piano and woodwinds pass back and forth as the music modulates. A march-like rhythm takes shape in the piano. It is later set against the returning first subject.
cues.evidence: Full score, first movement development; the emerging march-like idea and its later combination with the first subject are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._2_(Rachmaninoff).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First complete performance, Moscow, 1901
cues.text: Rachmaninoff was the soloist at the first complete performance in Moscow on 9 November 1901. His cousin and former teacher Alexander Siloti conducted. The Adagio and finale had already had a successful première, and the first movement was heard for the first time.
cues.evidence: Marc Mandel’s BSO note gives the complete première, Siloti’s relationship to Rachmaninoff and the earlier performance of the last two movements. https://www.bso.org/works/piano-concerto-no-2-6

cues.title: Recapitulation of the first subject
cues.text: The orchestra brings back the first theme in C minor. The piano plays hard, march-like chords against it in place of its original arpeggios, so the broad melody sounds above a repeated rhythm in the piano.
cues.evidence: Full score, first movement recapitulation; the march-like piano counterline against the returning first subject is described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._2_(Rachmaninoff).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Second melody, solo horn
cues.text: A solo horn plays the second melody in A♭ major, marked p dolce. The piano stops. The strings accompany with repeated pp chords under the horn’s long notes, following the march.
cues.evidence: Full score, p. 40, rehearsal 13: solo horn, p dolce, A♭ major and repeated pp string chords.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Coda, Meno mosso
cues.text: At the Meno mosso (rehearsal 16) the first theme returns pp in the strings over small piano figures. Rachmaninoff delays the final acceleration. The movement closes in C minor, and the concerto reaches C major only at the end of the finale.
cues.evidence: Full score, pp. 44–47, rehearsal 16 and conclusion: Meno mosso, pp strings and piano, then the C minor close; the finale ends in C major.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Piano chords become arpeggios at rehearsal 1
transitions.from: Intro · Piano chords over low F
transitions.how: The repeated low F moves to C, and the piano changes from solid chords to arpeggios. Violins, violas and clarinet begin the C minor theme, marked con passione in the strings. Cellos and double basses play the bass line pizzicato beneath the piano’s arpeggios.
transitions.evidence: Gutheil full score, Boosey & Hawkes reprint, pp. 3–4, rehearsal 1.

transitions.title: The piano takes the second melody
transitions.how: The quick più mosso piano passage moves through cadences towards E♭ major. The dynamic then drops and the piano plays the second melody, sustained above its own broken chords. Short woodwind phrases are heard around the solo line.
transitions.evidence: Full score, first movement transition and E♭ major second subject; structural account at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._2_(Rachmaninoff).

transitions.title: Exposition into development
transitions.to: Dev · Themes pass between piano and winds
transitions.how: The closing passage in E♭ major dies down. Woodwind phrases and piano figures take up fragments of both themes and repeat them over changing bass notes. The melody passes from one instrument to another, and the harmony moves away from the keys of the exposition.
transitions.evidence: Full score, first movement development; its use of both themes and changing orchestration is described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._2_(Rachmaninoff).

transitions.title: Into the C minor recapitulation
transitions.from: Dev · Themes pass between piano and winds
transitions.to: A′ · The tune returns against a march
transitions.how: The piano’s accelerating chords and the brass calls lead directly into the return of C minor. The orchestra plays the first melody again while the piano continues the march-like rhythm developed in the middle section. The first theme returns during the crescendo.
transitions.evidence: Full score, first movement development and recapitulation; the combination of first theme and march-like piano writing is described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._2_(Rachmaninoff).

transitions.title: Piano chord to solo horn
transitions.from: A′ · The tune returns against a march
transitions.how: The piano descends chromatically to an A♭ major chord at ppp. The piano then rests, and a solo horn plays the second subject, p dolce, as the strings repeat soft chords underneath. The horn plays the theme the piano had played earlier, in a single phrase.
transitions.evidence: Full score, pp. 39–40, rehearsal 13: descending piano line, A♭ major chord and solo horn.

transitions.title: The first theme returns at pp
transitions.to: Coda · Meno mosso, then C minor
transitions.how: Late in the movement the piano arpeggios touch C major, and the coda then turns back towards C minor. At Meno mosso the strings play the first theme again at pp. Above a slower-moving bass the piano plays short figures. The final drive to the end begins from this pp return.
transitions.evidence: Full score, pp. 44–47, rehearsal 16 and conclusion; the preceding C major arpeggios and C minor coda are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._2_(Rachmaninoff).

source.title: Rachmaninoff, Piano Concerto No. 2, I. Moderato, full score (Gutheil; Boosey & Hawkes reprint)
source.locator: Printed pp. 3–47, rehearsal figures 1–16: piano introduction, orchestral first theme, E♭ major piano melody, march-like return and A♭ major horn solo.

timeline.note: The piano’s repeated chords grow louder over a recurring low F.
Clarinet and upper strings play the C minor tune; cellos and basses play pizzicato beneath the piano arpeggios.
The string melody broadens, with wind and horn chords around the piano’s running notes.
Piano figures pass between held flute and clarinet chords and short horn and string answers.
The piano plays the second theme in E♭ major over quiet strings, with short answering phrases in the woodwind.
Woodwinds answer the piano; brass and timpani strengthen the exposition’s closing phrases.
Piano and woodwinds exchange fragments of the themes over held and repeated string chords.
Flutes and oboes play long notes against the piano’s quicker figures, supported by horns and lower strings.
Brass calls rise above the piano’s chords as the strings join the crescendo.
The orchestra brings back the first theme in C minor against marching chords in the piano.
The piano continues the tune as the brass falls silent and woodwinds answer over quieter strings.
A solo horn plays the second tune in A♭ major, with repeated string chords and the piano at rest.
The piano’s late arpeggios run between soft wind chords and sustained string lines.
At Meno mosso the strings, unmuted, play the first tune again, with quiet piano figures, bassoon and horn.
Winds, brass and timpani join piano and strings for the final C minor chords.

composer.epithet: Russian composer and pianist who earned his living at the piano in exile and whose music uses the sound of the bells of his childhood.
facts: Zverev and Siloti at the piano; Taneyev and Arensky in composition
Ivanovka, Dresden, New York, Villa Senar and Beverly Hills
Four piano concertos, three symphonies, three completed operas, choral music, songs and piano works

quote.text: I feel like a ghost wandering in a world grown alien. I cannot cast out the old way of writing, and I cannot acquire the new.
quote.source: Rachmaninoff to Leonard Liebling, 1939; published in The Musical Courier, 5 April 1943

composer.background:
“My hearty thanks to the old man for not having forgotten about me!” Rachmaninoff wrote to the singer Mikhail Slonov on 26 December 1892. The old man was Tchaikovsky, who had praised his opera Aleko in a newspaper interview. Rachmaninoff was nineteen and had recently graduated from the Moscow Conservatory with its Great Gold Medal. Tchaikovsky helped get the opera into the Bolshoi, and in May 1893 he sat in the audience and applauded.

His childhood had been less settled. He was born into a landowning family and grew up at Oneg, near Novgorod, until his father’s financial failures forced a move to St Petersburg. He entered the Conservatory there in 1883. His parents separated, his sister Sofia died of diphtheria, and his schoolwork went badly. His grandmother took him to Orthodox services, where he heard the choirs and bells he remembered all his life. In 1885 his cousin Alexander Siloti recommended that he move to Moscow to study with the piano teacher Nikolai Zverev, who was known for his strictness.
